title: Land-Based Knowledge and Constitutional Recognition
intro: Carpenter's land ethic meets the 1982 Constitution. Questions 69-72 are answered in this lesson — your writing saves here.

terms.def: Patriated constitution whose Section 35 recognizes and affirms existing Aboriginal and treaty rights, and first named Métis and Inuit as Aboriginal peoples.

body: Mushkegowuk Cree Elder James Carpenter states the land ethic plainly: he never heard Native people say they own the land. Land is for use and living, and abundance is shared, as when a fisher invites another to a rich spot. Title claims grow from that relationship, while rights claims grow from activities.

The Constitution Act fell short of leaders' hopes yet changed the field. For the first time Métis and Inuit were specifically recognized as Aboriginal peoples, and Section 35 gave every group a foothold for land claims and self-determination talks. Many leaders still worried the Charter's individual rights could press against collective rights, which is why question 70-71 answers must weigh support against concern.

The worry has a precise shape from Lesson 3. If the Charter protects individuals above all, then collective rights like a nation's fishery can look like discrimination against outsiders. Leaders feared courts would read Aboriginal rights through an individual lens and dissolve exactly what makes them Aboriginal: their group character.

Carpenter's ethic also answers how claims divide. Title claims grow from the land relationship itself; rights claims grow from activities on the land. Knowing which root a claim has tells you which evidence it needs: occupancy and exclusivity for title, integral continuing practice for rights.

example.title: See it in the questions
example.text: Question 69 asks for the most important aspect of the bush lifestyle in Carpenter's story. Answer from the ethic above: use and sharing within need, never ownership.

check.prompt: What did Section 35 change for Métis and Inuit peoples?
check.sample: Sample response: it named them as Aboriginal peoples for the first time and gave them a legal foothold for rights, claims, and self-determination talks.

title: Constitutional Negotiations and National Organizations
intro: Two accords and the united voice that faced them. Questions 73-75 are answered in this lesson — your writing saves here.

terms.def: The 1987 package recognizing Quebec as a distinct society. It ignored Aboriginal concerns and died when Elijah Harper's No blocked its extension.
The successor package that finally seated Aboriginal organizations at the table while cutting federal power.

body: The 1987 Meech Lake Accord recognized Quebec as a distinct society but ignored Aboriginal concerns, so Manitoba MLA Elijah Harper's single No blocked its extension and the accord expired. Harper, an Ojibwa-Cree legislator backed by the Assembly of First Nations, said killing the accord beat betraying Aboriginal peoples' concerns.

Charlottetown then seated the Assembly of First Nations, the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada, and the Métis National Council. Five national organizations now carry shared positions: the Assembly of First Nations, the Congress of Aboriginal Peoples, the Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, the Métis National Council, and the Native Women's Association of Canada.

Harper's No worked through procedure, not volume. Constitutional packages needed every legislature's approval against a deadline, so one legislature withholding its extension vote killed the whole accord. Harper, backed by the Assembly of First Nations, spent that single vote on the principle that no deal about Canada's future could skip its first peoples.

Charlottetown's lesson is the mirror: inclusion changed the text. With Aboriginal organizations at the table, self-government moved from ignored to negotiated, while the accord also cut federal power generally. Presence writes provisions; absence had written Meech Lake.

example.title: See it in the questions
example.text: Questions 73-75 ask for Harper's name and role, Charlottetown on self-government, and the five organizations. All three answers sit in the two paragraphs above.

check.prompt: Why did one MLA's No kill a national accord?
check.sample: Sample response: Meech Lake needed every legislature's approval on a deadline, and Harper refused the extension because the accord ignored Aboriginal concerns.

title: Aboriginal Title, Treaties, and Land-Related Constraints
intro: What title means and what reserve land cannot do. Questions 76-78 are answered in this lesson — your writing saves here.

terms.def: The legal right to exclusive use and occupancy of a specific, usually ancestral, territory.

body: Aboriginal title is the legal right to exclusive use and occupancy of ancestral territory, and First Nations could not give land the European way because their ethic was use and sharing rather than ownership. Carpenter's fisher sharing the rich spot shows a system with no sale in it.

The economics are concrete. Because reserve land cannot be sold or mortgaged, communities struggle to raise business capital or housing loans. That single restriction explains much of the pressure behind modern self-government and land-claim negotiations.

Title and treaty differ in what they protect. Aboriginal title is the legal right to exclusive use and occupancy of ancestral territory, proven through occupation. Treaties layer promises atop title questions: hunting guarantees, services, payments. Questions 76-78 test whether you can keep the layers separate while explaining why First Nations could no more sell land than sell kinship.

The mortgage trap follows directly. Banks lend against collateral they can seize and sell, but reserve land can be neither sold nor mortgaged, so neither businesses nor homebuyers can borrow normally. Economic development under those rules must come through claims, settlements, or self-government revenues instead.

example.title: See it in the questions
example.text: Questions 76-78 ask for title's definition, why land could not be given, and the sale problem. Answer all three from the two paragraphs above.

check.prompt: How does the no-sale rule connect to self-government pressure?
check.sample: Sample response: without sale or mortgage, communities cannot raise capital, so control over land and revenues through claims and self-government becomes the path to development.
